title: How does G1GC work (equal-sized regions, dynamic role assignment, Young/Mixed/Concurrent-Marking/Full phases, IHOP, MaxGCPauseMillis), and what makes it "Garbage First"?
shortTitle: How G1GC works — equal-sized regions, dynamic role assignment, Young/Mixed/Concurrent-Marking/Full phases, IHOP, MaxGCPauseMillis — and what makes it "Garbage First"

s1_definition.profdef: G1 (Garbage First) is a server-style, mostly-concurrent, region-based garbage collector that divides the heap into many equal-sized regions and dynamically assigns each region a role of Eden, Survivor, Old, or Humongous. It aims to meet a soft pause-time target (`-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis`) by collecting only as many regions as it can within that budget, prioritising the regions with the most reclaimable garbage first. It has been the default collector since Java 9.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the bank's giant document warehouse is split into hundreds of identical small rooms instead of two or three huge halls. A cleaning crew has a strict rule: "you get ten minutes, clean the rooms that are mostly trash first." They scan which rooms have the most throwaway paper and empty those first, because that frees the most space for the least effort. That is G1 — small equal rooms (regions), a time budget (pause target), and a greedy "most garbage first" strategy.
s1_definition.oneliner: G1 chops the heap into equal regions and greedily collects the ones with the most garbage first, trying to stay inside a pause-time budget.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** G1 (Garbage First) is a server-style, mostly-concurrent, region-based garbage collector that divides the heap into many equal-sized regions and dynamically assigns each region a role of Eden, Survivor, Old, or Humongous. It aims to meet a soft pause-time target (`-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis`) by collecting only as many regions as it can within that budget, prioritising the regions with the most reclaimable garbage first. It has been the default collector since Java 9.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the bank's giant document warehouse is split into hundreds of identical small rooms instead of two or three huge halls. A cleaning crew has a strict rule: "you get ten minutes, clean the rooms that are mostly trash first." They scan which rooms have the most throwaway paper and empty those first, because that frees the most space for the least effort. That is G1 — small equal rooms (regions), a time budget (pause target), and a greedy "most garbage first" strategy.

**One line to remember:** G1 chops the heap into equal regions and greedily collects the ones with the most garbage first, trying to stay inside a pause-time budget.

sections.s2_technical:
G1 splits the heap into equal-sized regions, typically between one and thirty-two megabytes, chosen so there are roughly two thousand regions. You can set the size with `-XX:G1HeapRegionSize=8m`. Unlike older collectors, Young and Old generations are not contiguous memory areas; they are just sets of regions that can be anywhere in the heap, and a region's role is assigned dynamically. A region that was Eden this cycle can become Old next cycle.

A young collection is a stop-the-world pause that evacuates live objects out of Eden and Survivor regions into new Survivor or Old regions, then frees the emptied regions entirely. Because evacuation copies survivors into fresh regions, G1 also compacts as it goes, which avoids the fragmentation that a non-moving collector suffers.

Concurrent marking runs mostly alongside the application to find which Old regions hold the most garbage. It starts at the Initial Mark (piggybacked on a young pause), then a concurrent Root Region Scan and Concurrent Mark, then a short Remark pause, and finally Cleanup which identifies completely empty Old regions and reclaims them immediately. `-XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent` (IHOP) controls when this marking kicks off; the default is forty-five percent of the heap, and modern G1 adjusts it adaptively.

A Mixed collection is the payoff: after marking knows the trash-richest Old regions, G1 collects all the Young regions plus a chosen slice of the most-garbage Old regions in the same pause, which is literally "garbage first." A Full GC is the fallback nobody wants — a single-threaded-ish, whole-heap, stop-the-world compaction that happens when G1 cannot keep up, usually because of allocation pressure or humongous-object churn, and it signals the collector is losing.

`-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis` is a soft goal, default two hundred milliseconds. G1 sizes the young generation and the number of Old regions in each Mixed collection to try to hit that target, trading throughput for latency. Setting it too low starves throughput because young generations shrink and collections become too frequent.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a transaction-enrichment service ingests a flood of payment events, builds a small enrichment object for each, and most of those objects die within milliseconds. The service must keep its ninety-ninth-percentile pause under two hundred milliseconds because the UPI switch times out slow responses. This is exactly how G1's young collection works — short-lived Eden objects are cheap to reclaim, and a pause-time target keeps the latency contract.

Problem 2 — Some payments reference a large customer profile cached in memory, and those profiles live for hours. Over time Old regions fill with a mix of still-live profiles and dead ones. This is exactly what concurrent marking plus Mixed collections solve — marking finds the trash-richest Old regions, and Mixed collections sweep them alongside the young ones.

Our mini-project is a runnable allocation simulator that mimics the enrichment service. It creates many short-lived enrichment objects and a few long-lived profile objects, prints the recommended G1 flags, and logs the before and after heap state so you can connect allocation behaviour to collector behaviour. The classes are `PaymentEnrichmentSimulator` (the main driver), `EnrichmentRecord` (short-lived), `CustomerProfile` (long-lived), and `HeapReporter` (reads the memory beans and logs usage).
sections.s4a_structure:
Project structure:

```
g1-tuning-demo/
├── pom.xml
├── run.sh
└── src/
    └── main/
        └── java/com/bank/jvm/g1/
            ├── PaymentEnrichmentSimulator.java   (main class + demo classes)
            └── HeapReporter.java
```

Configuration (JVM flags, not application config):

```bash
# g1-flags.conf — recommended G1 flags for the enrichment service
-XX:+UseG1GC
-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200        # soft pause target (default)
-XX:G1HeapRegionSize=8m         # explicit region size
-XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent=45   # IHOP: start concurrent marking at 45%
-Xms2g -Xmx2g                   # fixed heap avoids resize churn
-Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags
```
sections.s4e_build:
How you build and run it:

```bash
# Build
mvn -q clean package

# Run with the recommended G1 flags and GC logging
java -XX:+UseG1GC -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200 -XX:G1HeapRegionSize=8m \
     -Xms2g -Xmx2g -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags \
     -cp target/g1-tuning-demo-1.0.0.jar com.bank.jvm.g1.PaymentEnrichmentSimulator

# Inspect what G1 did: count young vs mixed pauses
grep "Pause Young"  gc.log | wc -l
grep "Pause Young (Mixed)" gc.log | wc -l
grep "Pause Full" gc.log   # should be ZERO in a healthy run
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two long-lived `CustomerProfile` objects (Rajesh SAV2001 and Priya CUR3001), and two million short-lived `EnrichmentRecord` objects created in a loop.

Step 1. The two profiles are allocated first. They are small but survive the whole run, so after a couple of young collections G1 promotes them from Eden through Survivor and finally into Old regions. The data itself does not change; only the region it lives in changes.

Step 2. Each loop iteration allocates one `EnrichmentRecord` with a sixteen-element int array. These land in Eden regions. The record is used immediately by `scoreRisk()` and then becomes unreachable.

Step 3. Eden fills up. G1 triggers a young stop-the-world pause. It copies the tiny set of still-live objects to Survivor regions and frees every emptied Eden region at once. Because almost all records are already dead, this pause is very short — this is the generational hypothesis paying off.

Step 4. As the run proceeds, Old-region occupancy creeps up past the IHOP threshold of forty-five percent. G1 starts concurrent marking in the background while the loop keeps running, identifying which Old regions hold mostly garbage.

Step 5. Once marking finishes, the next collections become Mixed: they evacuate young regions plus a slice of the trashiest Old regions in the same pause, reclaiming Old space without a Full GC. The live profiles are copied intact; the dead profile-referencing garbage is dropped.

Step 6. At the end, `HeapReporter` logs used and max heap. Used heap stays bounded because the collector kept pace. The gc.log shows many short young pauses, a few mixed pauses, and zero Full GCs.

```
Oct 25, 2026 1:40:11 AM com.bank.jvm.g1.PaymentEnrichmentSimulator main
INFO: Bank: National Bank of India — G1 enrichment simulator starting
Oct 25, 2026 1:40:11 AM com.bank.jvm.g1.HeapReporter report
INFO: Heap [before] used=12MB max=2048MB
Oct 25, 2026 1:40:12 AM com.bank.jvm.g1.HeapReporter report
INFO: Heap [during] used=74MB max=2048MB
Oct 25, 2026 1:40:14 AM com.bank.jvm.g1.PaymentEnrichmentSimulator main

Oct 25, 2026 1:40:14 AM com.bank.jvm.g1.HeapReporter report
```

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Allocation stream: 2,000,000 EnrichmentRecord + 2 CustomerProfile
    │
    ▼
  Eden regions (role: Young)
    │ fills to capacity
    ▼
  Young Pause (stop-the-world, short)
    │ copy survivors ───→ Survivor regions
    │ free emptied Eden regions (bulk)
    ├─ long-lived profiles age ───→ promoted to Old regions
    ▼
  Old-region occupancy rises
    │ crosses IHOP = 45%
    ▼
  Concurrent Marking (runs WITH the app)
    │ Initial Mark → Root Scan → Concurrent Mark → Remark → Cleanup
    │ ranks Old regions by garbage amount (most garbage FIRST)
    ▼
  Mixed Pause
    │ evacuate: all Young regions + trashiest Old regions
    │ live profiles copied intact, dead objects dropped
    ▼
  Heap bounded, zero Full GC   ← healthy outcome
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
G1, the Garbage First collector, has been the default since Java 9 and it works by dividing the heap into many equal-sized regions, usually sized so there are about two thousand of them, and it assigns each region a role of Eden, Survivor, Old, or Humongous dynamically rather than keeping the generations as fixed contiguous blocks. Because it copies live objects into fresh regions during every collection, it compacts as it goes and never suffers the old-generation fragmentation that a non-moving collector would.

The lifecycle has four parts. A young collection is a short stop-the-world pause that evacuates survivors out of Eden and frees the emptied regions in bulk. Concurrent marking runs mostly alongside the application and is triggered when heap occupancy crosses the Initiating Heap Occupancy Percent, forty-five percent by default; it finds which old regions are richest in garbage. A mixed collection then evacuates all the young regions plus a chosen slice of the trashiest old regions in one pause, and that is literally what "garbage first" means — it goes after the regions that give the most reclaimed space for the least work. The Full GC is the fallback that signals G1 has fallen behind, and in a healthy service you should see none.

The knob I reach for first is MaxGCPauseMillis, a soft target defaulting to two hundred milliseconds; G1 sizes the young generation and the number of old regions per mixed collection to try to honour it, trading some throughput for predictable latency. At National Bank of India I ran a payment-enrichment service where almost every object died within milliseconds, so the young collections were tiny and cheap, while a handful of cached customer profiles lived for hours and settled into old regions that mixed collections cleaned up without ever forcing a Full GC. I verified all of this by reading the gc logs and alerting on any Full GC and on the pause ninety-ninth percentile, which is exactly the discipline I bring to tuning any latency-sensitive JVM service.
